candidates.title: Show HN: Imza – plan and review focused coding agent
candidates.raw_content: Hi everyone. I've been building Imza for the last three months. It's yet another coding agent. I know there are a dozen have been posted here. But I believe this one is different enough to have a place here. It has three explicit modes: plan, build and review. Plan mode allows you to draft a spec document together with the agent. Both you and the agent can edit the document until everything is clear. Build mode takes the plan and implements it. Review mode provides you a code review tool. You can annotate things you want to change in the code and send them as revision to the plan mode. It's entirely written in C++, requires no account, supports 50+ providers including OpenAI subscriptions or local models. Imza supports MCP, skills and instruction files out of the box and uses 8-11MB RAM at startup. One of the biggest differentiator is the Lua engine. What I did differently here is agent receives only one tool, that allows the LLM to execute Lua scripts. I then passed C++ methods as Lua bindings that the agent can execute. So model can orchestrate multiple bindings in one call. Each binding passes through a permission layer. Since Lua is the only way to interact with the filesystem, imza can monitor and control the model's behavior. I'd love to hear your feedback. Thanks Website: https://imza.run Source: https://github.com/umutsevdi/imza Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50314538 Points: 2 # Comments: 0

candidates.title: Why Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI need their own AI detection tools
candidates.raw_content: I'm not naive enough to think that these companies don't already have some internal detection tools, but they clearly are not being used enough. Lately researching anything using agents has been a pain (especially if the query leads up to buying intent) - the sources quoted are often AI slop, which are then used to deterministically argue a point. On the first challenge to logic, the reply is usually an apology followed by a tangential search and agreement on the user argued point - sometimes even a hedge. There is a simple problem embedded at the center of this, that at least partially explains this degradation - AI generated text. There is now arguably more AI generated text on the web than human writings, and platforms that used to be very credible (attracting high quality technical writers) now seem to be full of AI generated slop (someone has to call them out). It's a pattern I'm sure most people are noticing under the hood - query -> beautiful prose -> suspect sources. You challenge the answer, and all of a sudden it's a wildly different conclusion. To me that just sounds unreliable, because you could potentially argue with it to generate any conclusion you want - doesn't sound like a reliable brainstorming partner anymore. Not to mention it's preference for believing structured AI prose output as high quality writing. Perhaps it is simply a byproduct of the baked in agreeability or "dooms-day" protections baked in to system prompts. This makes it even more important to have sources quoted by bots verified for authority and origin. The authority test is being easily faked by rampant SEO abuse on once reliable blogging platforms (I won't name them but you know who) - apparently one bot - sorry user - singing product praises is enough for chat to recommend that product, mind-boggling. And one biased - sorry tailored - article comparing a product to 5 competitors is enough to determine which is best. If this is not a crisis, idk what is. The detection problem: Using conventional techniques like duplicate detection, repetition and similarity filters on AI generated content is a lost cause - there's enough probabilistic variance in them to generate millions of different copies. One solution to the problem: Use an AI detector to adjust result ranks. By adjusting the ranking using AI generated labels, not only will engines prioritise genuine human writings - they also potentially refer to a wider range of opinions on a subject, improving diversity consulted in answers. I know it sounds like an over-simplification, and it probably is - but to me it does sound like a first step in the right direction. Taken from https://t9xt.com/writings/why-google-microsoft-anthropic-and-openai-need-to-build-their-own-ai-detection-tools-before-it-i Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50314217 Points: 1 # Comments: 0
